sections.title: The Beit Din in the Conversion Process
sections.html:
Although the essence of conversion is accomplished by the convert, who chooses to join the people of Israel, which is destined to bring the word of God and His blessing to the world, the conversion must be carried out before a beit din (rabbinical court). This is because changing the status of the convert is a legal act that has consequences for all of Israel, and therefore the conversion must be carried out by a beit din (Yevamot 47a). However, a small Sanhedrin of twenty-three judges is not required for this; rather, a beit din of three judges suffices, which is the smallest judicial bench that exists in Jewish law (Yevamot 46b; Sanhedrin 3a).1

The beit din is needed for all stages of the conversion. In the first stage, the beit din examines the convert's desire to enter the people of Israel and to accept the Torah and the mitzvot, and decides whether to accept him. In the second stage, the beit din must be present at the time of the brit mila (circumcision) for men, and at the time of the immersion for men and women. For since the conversion depends on circumcision and immersion, they too are included in the judicial act of conversion, and they must take place before a beit din of three. Therefore, one must also take care that the brit mila and the immersion take place during the day, for since conversion is considered a "judgment" (mishpat), just as the judgments of the Torah, including the session of the beit din to accept the convert, must take place during the day, so too all stages of the conversion must take place during the day (SA YD 268:3).2

sections.title: Who Is Fit to Serve as Judges
sections.html:
Ab initio, the judges of the conversion should be Torah scholars, so that they carry out the conversion according to halakha and properly weigh whether to accept the convert. After the fact, even if the judges of the conversion were not Torah scholars, as long as they were fit to testify, the conversion is valid. Those fit to testify are Torah-observant Jews who are not known to transgress deliberately any of the mitzvot of the Torah (below, halakha 9). Some say that even ab initio, Torah-observant Jews who are not Torah scholars may serve as the beit din for the entire conversion process, provided that one of them knows how to carry out the act of conversion according to halakha.

In practice, after the fact, if the judges were Torah-observant but not Torah scholars, the conversion has full validity. But ab initio, one should take care that the judges of the conversion be Torah scholars. And the custom of Israel is that the local rabbis are responsible for conversion, so that the acceptance of converts has the broad consent of the entire community. However, at the ceremony of the brit mila and the immersion, one may, even ab initio, make do with three fit Jews who serve as a beit din and supervise that the mitzva is performed according to halakha. This is because at the stage of circumcision and immersion the judges do not need to exercise discretion; rather, they continue the conversion process on the basis of the decision of the beit din that accepted the convert3

sections.title: It Is a Mitzva to Accept Righteous Converts
sections.html:
It is a mitzva to draw near and convert righteous converts (gerei tzedek), and therefore the Sages said that once it is known that the convert's desire to convert is a genuine desire, the conversion should not be delayed, for one should not tarry in fulfilling the mitzva (Yevamot 47b). Included in this mitzva is accompanying and teaching the righteous convert in preparation for his acceptance by the beit din. This mitzva is included in the mitzva of loving God and in the mitzva of loving one's fellow creatures.

Loving God, as it is stated (Devarim 6:5): "And you shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul and with all your might." The Sages said (ibid. in the Sifrei): "'And you shall love the Lord' – make Him beloved to His creatures," in the way that Avraham our father and Sarah our mother would draw converts near, as it is stated (Bereishit 12:5): "And the souls that they had made in Ḥaran." And what is meant by "made"? "Surely if all the inhabitants of the world gathered together to create a single gnat and put a soul into it, they could not!" So how could Avraham and Sarah make souls? "Rather, it teaches you that whoever draws a convert near, it is as if he created him … Avraham would convert the men and Sarah would convert the women" (Bereishit Rabba 39:14; 84:4).

Loving one's fellow creatures, because conversion involves an act of kindness toward the convert, who through conversion will merit to enter under the wings of the Shekhina and be elevated to the stature of Israel. Therefore, all those who help converts to convert fulfill thereby the mitzva of "And you shall love your fellow as yourself" (Vayikra 19:18), on top of which a special mitzva was added to love the convert, as it is stated (Devarim 10:19): "And you shall love the convert, for you were strangers in the land of Egypt" (above 1:1).4

sections.title: Conversion for the Sake of Benefits
sections.html:
Conversion must be for the sake of Heaven, that is, out of identification with Judaism; but if the gentile seeks to convert not for the sake of Heaven, he should not be accepted. Therefore, the beit din must clarify for what purpose the gentile has come to convert. If it becomes clear that he wishes to convert for the sake of marriage, that is, in order to marry a Jewish woman, or to improve his economic situation, he should not be accepted, since his conversion is not for the sake of Heaven. Therefore the Sages said (Yevamot 24b): "Converts are not accepted in the days of the Messiah," for then there is concern that the conversion is for the sake of honor and money. "Similarly, converts were not accepted either in the days of David or in the days of Shlomo." In the days of David, because they sought to convert out of fear of his armies, and in the days of Shlomo, because they sought to convert in order to share in the wealth of Israel. The Sages likewise said that "lion converts and dream converts" are not accepted, that is, people who do not identify with Judaism but come to convert out of fear – so that lions not kill them, or because an angel warned them in a dream to convert in order to be saved from calamity.

However, even in times when Israel merits wealth and honor, if the beit din has the impression that the convert's intention is for the sake of Heaven, he is accepted. Thus in the days of David they accepted Ittai the Gittite, for since he was wealthy and distinguished, it was clear that he came to convert for the sake of Heaven. It is likewise related (Menaḥot 44a) that they converted a woman who came to convert for the sake of marriage, because it became clear from her story that her main intention was for the sake of Heaven (Tosafot Yevamot 24b, s.v. "lo").5

If the beit din, deliberately or inadvertently, transgressed and accepted converts who did not come for the sake of Heaven, according to Rabbi Neḥemya their conversion has no validity. However, according to halakha, although ab initio one should not accept a convert who converts for the sake of marriage, if they accepted him, his conversion is a valid conversion, as explained in the Mishna (Yevamot 24b; SA YD 268:12. See above 3:9, note 8, regarding the conversion of the Kutim – the Samaritans).

sections.title: The Dilemma of the Beit Din
sections.html:
In order to understand the great dilemma that faces the beit din when it comes to decide on accepting a convert, let us return to the fundamentals. The purpose of conversion is to join the people of Israel, the people of God, whose destiny is to walk in the ways of God and to bring blessing to all the families of the earth. For this purpose God gave His people Israel His Torah and His mitzvot, through whose fulfillment it will merit His light and His blessing and will be able to repair the world.

The problem is that the beit din has no ability to know with certainty whether the convert wishes to convert out of faith in God and a desire to fulfill mitzvot, or whether he wishes to convert for the sake of benefits or in order to regularize his marriage. And although the convert declares his faith in God and his desire to fulfill mitzvot, the judges are unable to search the heart and mind and know whether he is speaking truth or falsehood, or whether his words are divided – partly true and partly false. And even in a case where the judges are inclined to think that the convert is speaking the truth, they are unable to know whether in practice the convert will withstand the difficulties involved in integrating into the people of Israel and in fulfilling the mitzvot, or whether, because of weakness of character or the difficulties he will encounter, he will weaken in his faith and stop fulfilling mitzvot, and perhaps even return to his previous identity. And conversely, even when the judges are inclined to suspect that the convert is lying, and he does not truly identify with Judaism and does not intend to fulfill mitzvot, and his request to convert is in order to regularize his marriage or his status in Israel, it is possible that over time, living among Israel, he will progress gradually to the level of a righteous convert. Experience, too, teaches that it is hard to predict the future, for there were converts who at first were very enthusiastic about Judaism, and after their conversion reverted to their old ways. And there were converts who appeared indifferent to Judaism, and were accepted with difficulty only because they were already living with a Jewish spouse, and after the conversion, in a gradual process, they grew greatly stronger until they became great tzaddikim.

If, in order to avoid accepting converts who will not be righteous converts, the beit din agrees to convert only converts who are almost certain to be righteous converts, it will sin by rejecting many converts who could have been righteous converts, and will cause great harm to the people of Israel. For the Sages said (Pesaḥim 87b): "The Holy One, blessed be He, exiled Israel among the nations only so that converts would be added to them"; thus rejecting a convert prolongs the exile and delays the redemption. Moreover, refusing to accept a convert whose soul is rooted in Israel may cause great danger to Israel, for this is a great soul that has not found its rectification, and it may turn to evil. As the Sages said about Timna, who was a princess and wished to cleave to the seed of Avraham our father and to convert. However, the Patriarchs rejected her, apparently because they sensed that her character traits were not good. She went and became a concubine to Elifaz the son of Esav, and from her was born Amalek, who caused Israel suffering. From here the Sages learned that after Timna came back and asked again and again to convert, the Patriarchs should have converted her and not pushed her away (Sanhedrin 99b; Bereishit Rabba 82:14). We have likewise learned that as a result of Avraham our father's negligence in converting the people of Sedom, it was decreed upon his descendants that they be enslaved in Egypt (Nedarim 32a; above 1:9, note 5).

On the other hand, if the beit din persuades gentiles to convert, or is lenient in converting anyone who asks, it will cause great harm to Israel by accepting converts who will continue to identify as gentiles and to behave according to their customs, and will influence for the worse their friends and neighbors, who will learn from their ways. Regarding such converts the Sages said (Yevamot 47b): "Converts are as difficult for Israel as a sapaḥat (a skin affliction)" (above 1:11, note 7), and regarding those who accept such converts they said (Yevamot 109b): "Evil after evil will come upon those who accept converts."

Many times the reality is complex: the convert's intention is not sufficiently for the sake of Heaven, and there is indeed concern that his conversion will cause troubles and complications, and perhaps he and his family members will influence their Jewish friends for the worse. However, there is also a chance that after a long and painful process, he and his descendants will become integrated into Israel and absorb the faith of Israel, and great and righteous people will come forth from them.

sections.title: The Approaches of Shammai and Hillel
sections.html:
The decision of the beit din also depends on the character and life experience of the judges. If they are inclined toward kindness and their approach is optimistic, or if they have encountered righteous converts in the past, they will tend to look upon the convert favorably and to believe that his intention is good, and they will accept him. And if they are inclined toward the attribute of strict judgment and their stance is sober and pessimistic, or if they have encountered in the past converts who turned out to be alienated from Israel and from the mitzvot, they will tend to doubt the convert's intention and will not agree to accept him.

Similarly, it is related in the Talmud (Shabbat 31a) about a certain gentile who came before Shammai and asked him: How many Torahs do you have? Shammai answered him: Two – the Written Torah and the Oral Torah. He said to him: The Written one – I believe you; but the Oral one – I do not believe you. Convert me on condition that you teach me the Written Torah. Shammai rebuked him and sent him away in reproach. He came before Hillel – he converted him and began to teach him, until he accepted upon himself the Oral Torah as well.

Another incident: a gentile came before Shammai the Elder and asked to convert on condition that he teach him the entire Torah while standing on one foot. Shammai pushed him away with the builder's cubit (measuring rod) that was in his hand, for how is it possible to teach the entire Torah on one foot?! As for his pushing him away with a builder's cubit – this is because such was the way of the greatest Sages: as long as they did not serve in public positions, they made their living from their own work. Hillel was a woodcutter and Shammai was a builder. By pushing the gentile away with the builder's cubit, with which he would straighten his building, Shammai hinted to him that his request was improper and deviated from the straight path. That gentile came before Hillel; he agreed to convert him, and said to him: What is hateful to you, do not do to your fellow – this is the entire Torah on one foot, and all the rest of the words of the Torah are explanations and ramifications of this great foundation, and you must go on to study them in order to fulfill the Torah.

Another incident: a certain gentile heard about the garments of the High Priest and was impressed by his honor and by the splendid beauty of his garments. He came before Shammai and asked to convert on condition that he be appointed High Priest. Shammai pushed him away with the builder's cubit that was in his hand, for one who was not born a kohen cannot be a High Priest. When he came before Hillel with the same request, Hillel accepted him and converted him, and told him that since he wishes to be a great man in Israel, he must study "the protocols of royalty," that is, the Torah. When the convert reached the verse in which it is explained that even Israelites cannot serve in the priesthood, he reasoned a kal va-ḥomer (a fortiori) regarding himself and understood that a convert cannot be High Priest, and he agreed to be an ordinary Jew.

The Sages concluded their story by relating that some time later these three converts happened to come together in one place, and they said: "Shammai's impatience sought to drive us from the world; Hillel's humility brought us near, under the wings of the Shekhina." Seemingly, according to the letter of the law, Shammai was right in not accepting these three converts, for according to their own words they did not accept the Torah and the mitzvot. In addition, it is reasonable that in contrast to those three converts whom Shammai rejected and Hillel accepted and who turned out to be righteous converts, there were cases in which Hillel accepted converts who afterward reverted to their old ways, and it turned out that Shammai had been right. However, from the fact that the Gemara chose to bring the story of the converts whom Hillel accepted and who turned out to be righteous converts, it is implied that it is preferable to follow the approach of Hillel. That is, although it is clear that there is room for the approach of Shammai, and every rabbi who resembles Shammai in his character and worldview should be faithful to his own way, the Gemara wished to teach us that the way of Hillel is preferable.

In the course of this we have learned that a convert, too, is permitted to choose to convert with rabbis who follow the way of Hillel, and even if he sought to convert with one rabbi who did not accept him, he may go to convert with another rabbi. And likewise a rabbi is permitted to accept a convert who was rejected by another rabbi.

sections.title: Everything According to the Judgment of the Beit Din
sections.html:
Since the beit din cannot know with certainty what is in the heart of the one converting, and cannot predict how the convert and his descendants will behave in the future, the beit din must weigh all the considerations and decide according to its discretion. That is, there is almost always some doubt whether it is right to accept the convert or to reject him, and the responsibility and the authority to decide according to what seems right in its eyes rests with the beit din, in accordance with the famous rule: "Everything is according to the judgment of the beit din" (Beit Yosef 268:12; Shakh 23).

There are situations in which the poskim disagree as to how far the beit din may use its authority and convert a convert regarding whom there is serious concern that his conversion is not for the sake of Heaven. Some are stringent and hold that when there is a well-founded doubt whether the one seeking to convert does not intend it for the sake of Heaven, it is obligatory to reject him, and the matter is not left to the discretion of the beit din. This, they say, is what the Sages (Yevamot 24b) meant in their instruction not to accept a convert who wishes to marry a Jewish woman, and not to accept converts at a time when Israel lives in wealth, for in these cases there is serious concern that the conversion is for the sake of marriage or money, and not for the sake of Heaven. Only when it seems very likely to the beit din that the convert's main intention is for the sake of Heaven and he intends to fulfill mitzvot with devotion, even though there is also a motive of marriage or money, may it exercise discretion and accept him.

On the other hand, some are lenient and hold that even where there is a well-founded concern that the convert's intention is not for the sake of Heaven, for instance he wishes to marry a Jewish woman or to improve his economic situation, if the beit din assesses that there is a chance that the convert will progress and become a righteous convert, it may convert him. Likewise, if through the conversion his partner will preserve her Jewish identity and be saved from assimilation, the beit din may decide to convert him, even though his main intention is to convert for the sake of marriage or money. For what the Sages said – not to convert for the sake of marriage or money – applies specifically when the convert's entire intention is for the sake of marriage or money; but if he also has an intention for the sake of Heaven, it is permitted to convert him. They further explained that not accepting converts for the sake of marriage is good guidance but not binding law, and when there is a special need for it in order to save from assimilation, or when the judges also see a good intention in the one converting, it is within their authority to decide to convert him even though the main motive for the conversion is not for the sake of Heaven.6

sections.title: A Beit Din of Laymen
sections.html:
As we learned (in halakha 4), the Sages said (Yevamot 24b): "Converts were not accepted either in the days of David or in the days of Shlomo." In the days of David because of the concern that they sought to convert out of fear of his armies, and in the days of Shlomo because of the concern that they sought to convert in order to share in the wealth of Israel. But this is difficult, for the Sages said (Yevamot 79a) that in the days of David and Shlomo one hundred and fifty thousand converts were converted, who saw how Israel treated the Givonite converts with honor and asked to convert, and they were the ones who helped Shlomo prepare the materials for building the Temple (above 3:7).

The Rambam explained (Issurei Bi'ah 13:15) that indeed the official batei din did not accept converts in the days of David and Shlomo; however, many converts would convert "before laymen, and the Great Beit Din was wary of them: they did not reject them, since they had immersed in any case, nor did they draw them near until their end would be seen" (and so wrote the Ramban and Rashba). According to the overwhelming majority of the poskim, there was no doubt about the validity of the conversion, for after the fact laymen are fit to convert; and what is meant by the Great Beit Din not drawing them near until it would see how they behaved is that they did not rely on their trustworthiness regarding kashrut, or that they recommended not marrying them, until they would see that they conducted themselves according to halakha.7

The poskim disagree as to what the attitude of the Great Beit Din was toward those batei din of laymen that converted the one hundred and fifty thousand converts. Some say that the Great Beit Din opposed their converting improperly, but since, after the fact, any Jew who is fit to testify is fit to serve as a judge for conversion, the conversion performed by the laymen was valid (Kesef Mishneh, Issurei Bi'ah 13:15; Ezrat Kohen 14).

And some say that the beit din did not oppose the conversions of the batei din of laymen, but rather preferred to turn a blind eye to their conversions, and perhaps even supported them silently. For it is impossible that it opposed and protested against them and nevertheless they converted one hundred and fifty thousand contrary to its position. Rather, its position was that it is not fitting for the Sages to convert converts who come to convert for the sake of security and wealth, but on the other hand, it is also not fitting to reject them. Therefore it preferred that laymen convert them, for they are permitted to respond to such converts and convert them (Maggid Mishneh, Issurei Bi'ah 13:14; Aderet Eliyahu YD 87).8

sections.title: A Valid and an Invalid Beit Din
sections.html:
As we learned (in halakha 2), ab initio the judges of conversion should be Torah scholars; however, after the fact, even Jews who are not Torah scholars are fit to be judges for conversion. This is the rule: anyone who is disqualified from being a witness in one of the official testimonies of the Torah, such as testimony for marriage or divorce, is disqualified from being a judge for conversion. And who is disqualified from testimony? One who is considered "wicked" with regard to one of the mitzvot, as it is stated (Shemot 23:1): "Do not put your hand with the wicked to be an unrighteous witness" (Sanhedrin 27a). That is, one who is known to transgress deliberately one of the mitzvot of the Torah. For example, a thief is disqualified from testimony, and if he returned the stolen item and repented fully of it, he becomes fit for testimony again. Similarly, if one of the judges of the conversion is known to take bribes, his conversions are invalid (see Baḥ ḤM 9:9). Likewise one who desecrates Shabbat or eats non-kosher food is disqualified from testimony, and if he repented, he becomes fit for testimony again (SA ḤM 34).

Therefore the poskim ruled that Reform, and even Conservative, conversion is invalid, since the converting judges do not observe all the mitzvot.9

When the Sages of a certain place enacted an ordinance that one may not convert there without certain conditions, as was done in the community of Sephardic Jews from Aleppo in Argentina, if Sages or laymen arose and converted contrary to the conditions they set, according to most poskim their conversions are valid. Admittedly, under certain conditions the representatives of the public may impose fines on those who convert contrary to the ordinances of the community, but they cannot invalidate the conversion, since it was carried out by Torah-observant Jews, whose status is at the very least that of laymen.10
